level.name: Elementary
level.description: Develop everyday English for familiar situations, past experiences, plans, comparisons, travel, and simple problem solving.

topics.title: Past Simple: Regular Verbs
topics.objective: Use regular verbs in the past simple to talk about completed past events.
topics.theory: Regular verbs usually form the past simple by adding -ed. Verbs ending in -e add -d. A consonant plus y often changes to -ied. Use the same past form with all subjects. Common time expressions include yesterday, last night, last week, and two days ago.
examples: She visited her aunt last weekend.

questions.option_d: I did watched a movie yesterday.
questions.explanation: Use the regular past form with a finished past time.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Tom walked to school and talked to his teacher.' What happened first?
questions.explanation: The sentence first states that he walked to school.

questions.prompt: Which time expression usually refers to the past?
Complete: They ___ tennis two hours ago.
What did the speaker do after work?
questions.explanation: The speaker says they visited a friend.
questions.audio_text: Yesterday, I finished work at five and visited a friend after dinner.

questions.explanation: The speaker says Anna studied math.
questions.audio_text: Anna studied math for two hours last night and finished her homework.

passages.title: A Busy Saturday
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did Eric do in the morning?
questions.explanation: He cleaned his apartment in the morning.
He played basketball in the park.

passages.content_text: Last Saturday, Eric stayed home in the morning. He cleaned his apartment, washed his clothes, and cooked lunch. In the afternoon, he walked to the park and played basketball with two friends. Later, they talked at a small café. Eric returned home at eight and watched a movie before bed.

passages.title: Last Weekend
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: On Sunday, Mia visited her grandparents. She helped them in the garden and cooked lunch with her grandmother. In the afternoon, they watched an old movie and talked about family photos. Mia returned home in the evening.

topics.title: Past Simple: Irregular Verbs
topics.objective: Use common irregular past forms to describe completed past events.
topics.theory: Irregular verbs do not form the past by simply adding -ed. Their forms must be learned, for example go/went, see/saw, eat/ate, have/had, buy/bought, take/took, and come/came.

questions.prompt: What is the past form of 'go'?
What is the past form of 'eat'?
Complete: We ___ a taxi to the airport.
Complete: She ___ a new jacket yesterday.
Read: 'Lisa had breakfast and went to work.' What did Lisa do after breakfast?
questions.explanation: She went to work after breakfast.

questions.prompt: Complete: They ___ us a nice gift.

questions.audio_text: I went to the station this morning and bought a ticket for the ten o'clock train.
My cousin came to dinner last night. We had pasta and talked for hours.

passages.title: A Surprise Trip
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How did Carla travel to Lisbon?

passages.content_text: Last month, Carla went to Lisbon with her brother. They took an early flight and arrived before noon. They had lunch near the river and saw several old buildings. Carla bought postcards for her family. In the evening, they found a small restaurant and ate local food.

passages.title: An Unexpected Morning
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did the manager give the speaker?

passages.audio_text: This morning, I woke up late because my alarm did not ring. I got dressed quickly, took a bus, and arrived at work twenty minutes late. My manager was understanding. She gave me a coffee and told me not to worry.

topics.title: Past Simple Questions and Negatives
topics.objective: Form past simple negatives and questions with did and didn't.
topics.theory: Use did not/didn't + base verb for negatives and Did + subject + base verb for questions. The main verb stays in the base form after did or didn't.

questions.explanation: Use 'Did' for a past simple question.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct answer to 'Did he come?'
Read: 'Maya didn't work on Monday. She stayed home.' What did Maya NOT do?
Did the speaker go to the party?
questions.explanation: The speaker says they didn't go.
questions.audio_text: I didn't go to the party last night because I was tired.

questions.explanation: The audio uses a correct past question.
questions.audio_text: Mark asked, Did you finish the report yesterday?

passages.title: Missed Plans
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why didn't Laura go to the café?

passages.content_text: Laura planned to meet her friend Ben on Friday evening, but she didn't go to the café. Her car didn't start, so she called Ben. He didn't answer his phone at first. Ten minutes later, he called her back. They decided to meet on Saturday instead.

passages.title: A Customer Call
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did the customer do this morning?

passages.audio_text: Did you receive my order yesterday? No, I didn't. The package didn't arrive. Did you check the tracking number? Yes, I did, but the website didn't show any new information. I called customer service this morning.

topics.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
topics.objective: Distinguish countable and uncountable nouns and use appropriate quantity expressions.
topics.theory: Countable nouns can be singular or plural and can use a/an and numbers. Uncountable nouns generally do not have a plural form and are used with expressions such as some, much, a little, or a piece of.

questions.prompt: Read: 'We bought two oranges and some rice.' Which noun is uncountable?
What uncountable item does the speaker need?
questions.audio_text: I need three eggs, two apples, and some milk for breakfast.

questions.explanation: The speaker says a loaf of bread.
questions.audio_text: Please buy a loaf of bread and two bottles of water.

passages.title: Preparing Dinner
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How many tomatoes does Nina have?

questions.explanation: Use 'two loaves of bread' or 'some bread'.

passages.content_text: For dinner, Nina needs several ingredients. She has two tomatoes, one onion, and some rice. She also has a little cheese, but she doesn't have any bread. Her brother is going to buy a loaf of bread and a bottle of olive oil.

passages.title: At the Grocery Store
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: We need some fruit and a few vegetables. Please get four bananas, three carrots, and some cheese. We also need a bottle of juice and a little sugar. Don't buy rice because we already have some at home.

topics.title: Some, Any, Much, Many, and A Lot Of
topics.objective: Use common quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns.
topics.theory: Use some mainly in affirmative statements and any mainly in negatives and many questions. Use many with countable plural nouns and much with uncountable nouns. A lot of works with both.

questions.explanation: Use many with countable plural nouns.

questions.prompt: Complete: How ___ time do we have?

questions.explanation: A lot of can be used with plural countable nouns.

questions.prompt: Read: 'We have some bread but we don't have any cheese.' What is missing?
What does the speaker have a lot of?
questions.explanation: The speaker says they have a lot of books.
questions.audio_text: I have a lot of books at home, but I don't have much free time to read them.
We have many apples, but we don't have any water.

passages.title: Planning a Picnic
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What do they have a lot of?
questions.explanation: They have a lot of food.

questions.prompt: What are they going to buy?
questions.explanation: Alex is going to buy plates.

passages.content_text: We have a lot of food for the picnic. There are many sandwiches and some fruit. We also have a lot of juice, but we don't have any water. There aren't many plates, so Alex is going to buy some. We don't need much sugar because nobody drinks sweet coffee.

passages.title: Kitchen Check
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: Do we have any pasta? Yes, we have some, but not much. How many tomatoes are there? There are four. We don't have any cheese, but there's a lot of yogurt in the refrigerator.

topics.title: Comparatives
topics.objective: Compare two people, places, or things using comparative adjectives.
topics.theory: Short adjectives usually add -er, while longer adjectives often use more. Use than after a comparative when naming the second item. Some forms are irregular, such as good/better and bad/worse.
examples: My car is faster than yours.
This book is more interesting than that one.

questions.prompt: Complete: A train is usually ___ than a bus.
Complete: This hotel is ___ than that one.
Read: 'The red phone costs $500. The blue phone costs $350.' Which is cheaper?

questions.option_a: My house is bigger than yours.
questions.option_b: My house is more bigger than yours.
questions.option_c: My house is biggest than yours.

questions.audio_text: Berlin is colder than Rome in winter, but Rome is usually sunnier.
The black bag is bigger, but the brown bag is cheaper.

passages.title: Choosing an Apartment
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.
passages.content_text: Lisa is comparing two apartments. Apartment A is closer to her office and cheaper than Apartment B. Apartment B is larger and more modern, but it is also noisier because it is near a busy road. Lisa thinks Apartment A is more practical for her daily life.

passages.title: Two Restaurants
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: The Green Café is smaller than Bella's Restaurant, but it is quieter. Bella's is more expensive, but the menu is larger. I think the food at the Green Café is better.

topics.title: Superlatives
topics.objective: Describe the highest or lowest degree in a group using superlative adjectives.
topics.theory: Use the + adjective-est with many short adjectives and the most + adjective with many longer adjectives. Irregular forms include best and worst.
examples: Mount Everest is the highest mountain.
This is the most expensive hotel.
She is the best student in the class.

questions.prompt: Complete: This is ___ restaurant in town.

questions.option_a: She is the youngest in the family.
questions.option_b: She is younger in the family.

questions.prompt: Three hotels cost $90, $120, and $200. Which is the most expensive?
Complete: January is usually ___ month here.

questions.explanation: Route C is described as the shortest.
questions.audio_text: Route A is long, Route B is shorter, and Route C is the shortest way to the station.
Anna is twenty, Mia is twenty-two, and Tom is twenty-five. Tom is the oldest.

passages.title: City Guide
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Which park has the most beautiful view according to many people?
questions.explanation: Hill Park has the most beautiful view.

passages.content_text: Our city has three popular parks. River Park is the largest. Central Park is the busiest because it is downtown. Hill Park is the smallest, but many people think it has the most beautiful view. On weekends, Central Park is usually the most crowded.

passages.title: Class Results
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: In our class, Emma got ninety-eight points, Leo got ninety-four, and Sara got eighty-seven. Emma got the highest score. Sara's test was the most difficult for her because grammar was her weakest area.

topics.title: Future with Going To
topics.objective: Talk about future plans and intentions using be going to.
topics.theory: Use am/is/are + going to + base verb for plans and intentions. It can also describe predictions based on present evidence.
examples: They are going to travel next month.
She isn't going to work tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Complete: I ___ going to cook tonight.
Complete: They are going to ___ next week.
questions.explanation: Use the base verb after going to.
Use isn't going to + base verb.

questions.prompt: Complete: We ___ going to visit our aunt.
Read: 'Ben bought paint because he is going to paint his room.' What is Ben's plan?
questions.explanation: His plan is to paint his room.

questions.prompt: Which phrase shows a future plan?

questions.option_a: I'm going to meet Sara tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Use am going to + base verb.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker going to do Saturday?
questions.explanation: The speaker plans to visit family.
questions.audio_text: I'm going to visit my parents on Saturday and stay for dinner.

questions.prompt: Where are they going to travel?
questions.audio_text: We're going to travel to Paris next month for four days.

passages.title: Weekend Plans
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What is Olivia going to do Saturday morning?
Who is she going to meet?
questions.explanation: She is going to meet two friends.

questions.option_b: She is going to meet friends.

passages.content_text: Olivia has a busy weekend. On Saturday morning, she is going to clean her apartment. In the afternoon, she is going to meet two friends at a café. On Sunday, she is going to visit her parents. They are going to cook lunch together and watch a movie.

passages.title: Holiday Preparation
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When are they going to leave?
Who is going to check the train times?

passages.audio_text: We're going to leave early tomorrow morning. I'm going to pack tonight, and my sister is going to check the train times. Our parents are going to drive us to the station.

topics.title: Will for Predictions and Decisions
topics.objective: Use will for simple predictions, promises, offers, and decisions made at the moment of speaking.
topics.theory: Use will + base verb. Common contractions include I'll, you'll, he'll, she'll, we'll, and they'll. Negative form: won't.

questions.prompt: Complete: I think it ___ rain tomorrow.
Complete: Don't worry. I ___ help you.

questions.explanation: Use the base verb after will.

questions.prompt: Read: 'The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.' Why does the speaker use will?
questions.explanation: The decision is made at the moment.

questions.prompt: Which word often introduces a prediction?
What does the speaker offer to do?
questions.explanation: The speaker offers to carry the bag.
questions.audio_text: That bag looks heavy. I'll carry it for you.
Look at those dark clouds. I think it will rain soon.

passages.title: Tomorrow's Technology
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What will people probably use to control things?

passages.content_text: Some people think homes will become smarter in the future. Lights will turn on automatically, and appliances will use less energy. People will probably control many things with their phones. However, experts say technology won't replace every human task.

passages.title: Quick Decisions
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What will the speaker turn on?
questions.explanation: The speaker will turn on the light.

passages.audio_text: I'm thirsty. I'll get some water. Do you want some? Yes, please. I'll have a glass too. The kitchen is dark. I'll turn on the light. Thanks. I'll wait here.

topics.title: Present Perfect: Introduction
topics.objective: Use the present perfect for life experiences and recent actions connected to the present.
topics.theory: Form the present perfect with have/has + past participle. At A2, common uses include life experiences with ever/never and recent actions with already/just/yet.

questions.prompt: Complete: Have you ___ been to Canada?

questions.explanation: Use 'never' for an experience that has not happened.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Lena has just arrived.' Is Lena here now?
questions.explanation: 'Has just arrived' connects a recent action to the present.
'Yet' is common in negatives and questions.

questions.audio_text: I've traveled by train many times, but I've never flown on a plane.
Maria has just arrived home, so she's taking off her coat now.

passages.title: Travel Experiences
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How many countries has Kevin visited?

questions.explanation: He has never traveled to Asia.

questions.option_b: He has never traveled to Asia.
questions.option_c: He has already been to France.

passages.content_text: Kevin loves travel. He has visited five countries and has taken many train trips. He has never traveled to Asia, but he wants to go there one day. He has already been to France twice, and he has just returned from a weekend in Belgium.

passages.title: Experiences with Food
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Has the speaker tried Indian food?
What has the speaker just bought?
questions.explanation: The speaker has just bought a cookbook.

passages.audio_text: Have you ever tried Indian food? Yes, I have. I've tried it several times. Have you ever cooked it? No, I haven't. But I've just bought a cookbook, so I want to learn.

topics.title: Adverbs of Manner
topics.objective: Describe how actions happen using common adverbs of manner.
topics.theory: Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to an adjective, for example slow/slowly and careful/carefully. Some forms are irregular, such as good/well and fast/fast.

questions.prompt: Read: 'The nurse spoke calmly to the patient.' How did she speak?

questions.audio_text: My father drives very carefully, especially when it rains.
The child listened to the teacher and answered politely.

passages.title: A Music Lesson
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How did the teacher explain the exercises?

passages.content_text: During the lesson, the teacher played the piano beautifully. She explained each exercise slowly and clearly. The students listened carefully. One student played very well, while another played too quickly and made several mistakes.

passages.title: A Careful Worker
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How does he speak to customers?

passages.audio_text: Sam works carefully because he repairs computers. He checks each part slowly, writes notes clearly, and speaks politely to customers. He usually finishes jobs quickly without making many mistakes.

topics.title: Object Pronouns
topics.objective: Use me, you, him, her, it, us, and them as objects of verbs and prepositions.
topics.theory: Object pronouns receive the action. Use me, you, him, her, it, us, and them after verbs and prepositions.

questions.prompt: Complete: I bought the book for ___.
Read: 'I saw Anna and Ben, so I spoke to them.' Who does 'them' refer to?
Complete: Where is my phone? I can't find ___.

questions.audio_text: I met Daniel at the station and gave him the tickets.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker buy for the children?
questions.explanation: The speaker bought something for them.
questions.audio_text: The children needed notebooks, so I bought them some after school.

passages.title: A Family Visit
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.
passages.content_text: My cousins visited us last weekend. We met them at the station and took them home. My mother cooked dinner for them. On Sunday, I showed them the city center. They thanked us before they left.

passages.title: Helping a Friend
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.
passages.audio_text: I couldn't find my keys, so I called Maya. She helped me look for them. We found them under the sofa. I thanked her and bought her a coffee.

topics.title: Should and Shouldn't
topics.objective: Give simple advice and recommendations using should and shouldn't.
topics.theory: Use should + base verb to give advice and shouldn't + base verb to advise against something.
examples: You shouldn't drive when you're tired.

questions.prompt: Complete: You ___ stay up all night.

questions.option_c: He should to see a doctor.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Sam has a headache. He should drink water and rest.' What advice is given?
Complete: We ___ be late for the appointment.
Choose the best advice for someone who is tired.

questions.audio_text: You look exhausted. You should go home and rest.
Alex is very tired, so he shouldn't drive tonight.

passages.title: Health Advice
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How long should Ben stay home?
questions.explanation: He should stay home for two days.

passages.content_text: Ben has a cold. His doctor says he should stay home for two days, drink plenty of water, and sleep more. He shouldn't exercise hard, and he shouldn't go to work while he has a fever.

passages.title: Advice for an Exam
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.explanation: The advice is not to study until 3 a.m.

passages.audio_text: You have an exam tomorrow. You should review your notes tonight, but you shouldn't study until three in the morning. You should prepare your bag before bed and get enough sleep.

topics.title: Travel and Directions
topics.objective: Ask for and understand simple travel information and directions.
topics.theory: Useful travel language includes turn left/right, go straight, get on/off, platform, ticket, departure, arrival, next to, across from, and between.
examples: Which platform does the train leave from?
Get off at the next stop.

questions.prompt: Where do trains usually leave from?
What do you do when you leave a bus?
Read: 'The museum is across from the station.' Where is it?

questions.option_a: Which platform does the train leave from?

questions.prompt: What do you usually need before boarding a train?

questions.audio_text: Go straight for one block, then turn right at the pharmacy.
The train to Oxford leaves from platform six at ten fifteen.

passages.title: Finding the Hotel
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What is next to the hotel?
questions.explanation: A pharmacy is next to it.

passages.content_text: From the train station, walk straight along King Street for about five minutes. Turn left at the bank. The Grand Hotel is on your right, next to a pharmacy and across from a small park. The entrance is on Queen Street.

passages.title: At the Station
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Which platform does the train use?

questions.explanation: The speaker says it is direct.

passages.audio_text: Excuse me, which platform is the train to Bristol? Platform four. It leaves at eleven twenty. Do I need to change trains? No, it's direct. Great. And what time does it arrive? At twelve forty-five.

topics.title: Everyday Problems and Solutions
topics.objective: Describe common everyday problems and respond with simple solutions or requests.
topics.theory: Useful language includes 'There's a problem with...', 'It doesn't work', 'I can't find...', 'Could you help me?', 'You should...', and 'I'll...'. Combine problem descriptions with polite requests and simple advice.

questions.explanation: It states that the phone is not working.

questions.prompt: If you can't find your keys, they may be ___.
questions.explanation: Lost means you cannot find them.

questions.prompt: What can you do if a computer freezes?
Read: 'The sink is leaking, so Maya called the building manager.' What is the problem?
Who can help with a problem with a purchased product?

questions.option_b: You should carry a heavy box.

questions.audio_text: The office printer is broken. It turns on, but it doesn't print anything.

questions.explanation: The speaker can't find the keys.
questions.audio_text: I can't find my keys. I've checked my bag and my desk, but they're not there.

passages.title: A Problem at Home
passages.instructions: Read the text carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When did the repair worker come?
questions.explanation: The worker came the next morning.

questions.option_c: He told her to turn off the water.
questions.option_d: He told her to turned off the water.

passages.content_text: On Monday evening, Sofia noticed that her kitchen sink was leaking. She put a bucket under it and called the building manager. He couldn't come that night, so he told her to turn off the water under the sink. A repair worker came the next morning and fixed the problem.

passages.title: Customer Service
passages.instructions: Listen to the passage and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What should the customer try first?
questions.explanation: The representative suggests restarting the phone.

passages.audio_text: Hello, I'm calling because my new headphones don't work. Have you charged them? Yes, I have. Have you tried restarting your phone? No, I haven't. Please try that first. If they still don't work, bring them to the store with your receipt.
